§12

Towards the exam

exam

The Linear Algebra and Geometry exam (part 2 of MDAG) is written and is the same for channels A, B and C. As of 30/09/2026 the 2026/27 rules have not been published yet: on Moodle it says "informazioni seguono" ("information to follow"). So the reference is the 2025/26 rules, confirmed by the exam papers.

What the exam looks like

  • 10 multiple-choice questions. Each has 5 answers, from (a) to (e), and only one is correct. Each question is worth 1 point.
  • 2 open problems, split into several questions. Each is worth 11 points. To get partial credit you must write down the steps.
  • Cut-off (sbarramento). The problems are marked only for those who score at least 6 points out of 10 in the quiz.
  • Duration: 2 hours. The maximum is 32 points, the pass mark is 18.
  • Materials allowed: only one folded sheet, or two A4 sheets (4 sides), handwritten, with formulas, notes and exercises. No calculator and no books.
  • In the quiz the answers are marked with an X, not with a circle.
2026/27 exam sessionRegistration on MyUniToTime and rooms
Fri 22/01/202702/01 – 15/01/202714:00, rooms A, B, C, D, F
Fri 05/02/202716/01 – 29/01/202714:00, rooms A, B, C, D, F

The final MDAG grade is the average of the two tests, Discrete Mathematics and Linear Algebra. They can also be taken in different exam sessions. Careful: sitting again a test you have already passed cancels the previous grade, even if it goes worse. Details and sources in the course sheet.

What you need from this lesson

  1. Fields. From lesson L05 every vector space is built "over a field". Being able to say why Z\ZZ is not a field is a typical theory question of the quiz.
  2. Notation. Sets, intervals, points and vectors with the right brackets. In the problems the answers are written with this notation.
  3. Calculations by hand. Fractions and roots appear in almost every question on lengths, angles and distances. Practise now with exercises 5 and 10.
  4. Reasoning by contradiction. The quiz does not ask for proofs, but this way of reasoning comes back often in the handouts.

Matters in the exam · The 4-page sheet

It is the only material allowed, so it is worth building it lesson by lesson. From this lesson two things are enough: the table of the rules for roots and the line "field = 9 rules; N\NN and Z\ZZ are not fields".

§13

Quiz

like the exam
  1. Which of these sets, with the usual sum and product, is not a field?
    In a field every number different from zero must have its inverse inside the set (rule 8). In Z\ZZ the inverse of 222 would be 12\frac 1221​, which is not an integer. So Z\ZZ is not a field. Q\QQ, R\RR and C\CC are.
  2. Which of these numbers is irrational?
    12=23\sqrt{12} = 2\sqrt 312​=23​, and 3\sqrt 33​ is irrational because 3 is not a perfect square. The others are all fractions: 0.125=180.125 = \frac 180.125=81​, 9=3\sqrt 9 = 39​=3, 0.3‾=130.\overline 3 = \frac 130.3=31​. 227\frac{22}7722​ is a fraction too: it is only a number close to π\piπ, it is not π\piπ.
  3. Which statement is true?
    Each family is inside the next and the next has something more: −1-1−1 is an integer but not a natural, 12\frac 1221​ is a rational but not an integer, 2\sqrt 22​ is a real but not a rational.
  4. The set {x∈R∣1≤x<2}\{x \in \R \mid 1 \le x < 2\}{x∈R∣1≤x<2} is:
    The symbol ≤\le≤ includes 1: square bracket on the left. The symbol <<< excludes 2: round bracket on the right. {1,2}\{1, 2\}{1,2}, on the other hand, is the set with just the two numbers 1 and 2.
  5. The number 0.999…0.999\ldots0.999… (with infinitely many digits 9) is equal to:
    Start from 13=0.333…\frac 13 = 0.333\ldots31​=0.333… and multiply both sides by 3: on the left you get 111, on the right 0.999…0.999\ldots0.999… They are two ways of writing the same number, like 5.9739‾5.973\overline 95.9739 and 5.9745.9745.974 in the handouts.
  6. In the proof that 2∉Q\sqrt 2 \notin \Q2​∈/Q, which contradiction is reached?
    From a2=2b2a^2 = 2b^2a2=2b2 we get that aaa is even. Substituting a=2ka = 2ka=2k we get that bbb is even too. Then top and bottom can be divided by 2, but the fraction had been chosen reduced: the two things cannot both be true.
  7. Which property does Z\ZZ lack to be a field?
    The "multiplicative inverse" is the inverse for the product, the one of rule 8. In Z\ZZ every number has its opposite, and all the other rules hold. But only 111 and −1-1−1 have an integer inverse: for example the inverse of 333 would be 13\frac 1331​.
  8. What is the value of 8+18\sqrt 8 + \sqrt{18}8​+18​?
    Take a square out of each root: 8=4⋅2=22\sqrt 8 = \sqrt{4 \cdot 2} = 2\sqrt 28​=4⋅2​=22​ and 18=9⋅2=32\sqrt{18} = \sqrt{9 \cdot 2} = 3\sqrt 218​=9⋅2​=32​. Now the roots are equal and can be added: 22+32=522\sqrt 2 + 3\sqrt 2 = 5\sqrt 222​+32​=52​. The answer 26\sqrt{26}26​ is the trap: the root of a sum is not the sum of the roots.
  9. What is the value of a2a_2a2​ in the sequence an=(1+1n)na_n = \left(1 + \frac 1n\right)^nan​=(1+n1​)n? Write a fraction or a decimal.
    9/4
    Put 2 in place of nnn. Inside the brackets: 1+12=321 + \frac 12 = \frac 321+21​=23​. Then the square: 32⋅32=94=2.25\frac 32 \cdot \frac 32 = \frac 94 = 2.2523​⋅23​=49​=2.25.
§14

Exercises

with solutions

1 · True or false with the symbols basic

Say whether each statement is true or false: (a) −3∈N-3 \in \N−3∈N; (b) 12∈Q\frac 12 \in \Q21​∈Q; (c) N⊂Z\N \subset \ZN⊂Z; (d) 9∈N\sqrt 9 \in \N9​∈N; (e) {2,4}⊂{1,2,3}\{2, 4\} \subset \{1, 2, 3\}{2,4}⊂{1,2,3}.

Solution

(a) False. −3-3−3 has the minus sign, and the naturals are 0,1,2,…0, 1, 2, \dots0,1,2,… So −3∉N-3 \notin \N−3∈/N.

(b) True. 12\frac 1221​ is a fraction with the number below different from zero.

(c) True. Every natural number is also an integer.

(d) True. Work it out first: 9=3\sqrt 9 = 39​=3. And 3 is a natural number.

(e) False. 2 is in {1,2,3}\{1, 2, 3\}{1,2,3}, but 4 is not. One element outside is enough.

2 · Opposites and inverses basic

For each number write the opposite and the inverse: (a) 333; (b) −12-\frac 12−21​; (c) 54\frac 5445​.

Solution

The opposite is the number that added gives 0: you change the sign. The inverse is the number that multiplied gives 1: in a fraction you swap top and bottom.

(a) Opposite of 333: −3-3−3, because 3+(−3)=03 + (-3) = 03+(−3)=0. Inverse: 13\frac 1331​, because 3⋅13=13 \cdot \frac 13 = 13⋅31​=1.

(b) Opposite of −12-\frac 12−21​: 12\frac 1221​, because −12+12=0-\frac 12 + \frac 12 = 0−21​+21​=0. Inverse: −2-2−2, because −12⋅(−2)=22=1-\frac 12 \cdot (-2) = \frac 22 = 1−21​⋅(−2)=22​=1.

(c) Opposite of 54\frac 5445​: −54-\frac 54−45​. Inverse: 45\frac 4554​, because 54⋅45=2020=1\frac 54 \cdot \frac 45 = \frac{20}{20} = 145​⋅54​=2020​=1.

3 · From the smallest to the biggest basic

Put in order from the smallest to the biggest: 222, −3-3−3, 12\frac 1221​, 000, −13-\frac 13−31​.

Solution

Think of the number line: further left means smaller.

  1. The negatives are to the left of zero. They are −3-3−3 and −13-\frac 13−31​. Of the two, −3-3−3 is further left: −3<−13-3 < -\frac 13−3<−31​.
  2. Then comes 000.
  3. The positives are to the right of zero. They are 12\frac 1221​ and 222, and 12<2\frac 12 < 221​<2.

Result: −3<−13<0<12<2-3 < -\frac 13 < 0 < \frac 12 < 2−3<−31​<0<21​<2.

Check of one step with the precise rule: −13−(−3)=−13+3=83-\frac 13 - (-3) = -\frac 13 + 3 = \frac 83−31​−(−3)=−31​+3=38​, which is positive. So −13>−3-\frac 13 > -3−31​>−3.

4 · Where each number lives basic

For each number find the smallest set among N\NN, Z\ZZ, Q\QQ, R\RR that contains it:

−4,0,72,16,7,0.12‾,π,−255.-4, \qquad 0, \qquad \frac 72, \qquad \sqrt{16}, \qquad \sqrt 7, \qquad 0.\overline{12}, \qquad \pi, \qquad -\frac{\sqrt{25}}{5}.−4,0,27​,16​,7​,0.12,π,−525​​.
Solution

The golden rule: simplify first, then decide.

NumberSimplifiedSmallest setWhy
−4-4−4−4-4−4Z\ZZit is negative, so it is not in N\NN
000000N\NNin the course zero is a natural
72\frac 7227​3.53.53.5Q\QQit is a fraction that is not an integer
16\sqrt{16}16​444N\NN4⋅4=164 \cdot 4 = 164⋅4=16
7\sqrt 77​cannot be simplifiedR\RR7 is not a perfect square: irrational
0.12‾0.\overline{12}0.12433\frac 4{33}334​Q\QQthe digits repeat, so it is a fraction (exercise 5)
π\piπcannot be simplifiedR\RRirrational
−255-\frac{\sqrt{25}}5−525​​−55=−1-\frac 55 = -1−55​=−1Z\ZZ25=5\sqrt{25} = 525​=5, then 5 divided by 5 is 1

16\sqrt{16}16​ looks like a "difficult" number, but it is 4.

5 · From a repeating decimal to a fraction basic

Write as a fraction: (a) 0.7‾0.\overline 70.7; (b) 2.3‾2.\overline 32.3; (c) 0.12‾0.\overline{12}0.12.

Solution

The trick is always the same. Call the number xxx. Multiply it by 10, so that the point moves one place. Then subtract xxx: the digits after the point are identical and cancel out.

(a) x=0.777…x = 0.777\ldotsx=0.777…

  1. I multiply by 10: 10x=7.777…10x = 7.777\ldots10x=7.777…
  2. I subtract: 10x−x=7.777…−0.777…=710x - x = 7.777\ldots - 0.777\ldots = 710x−x=7.777…−0.777…=7.
  3. On the left 10x−x10x - x10x−x is 9x9x9x. So 9x=79x = 79x=7.
  4. I divide by 9: x=79x = \frac 79x=97​.

(b) x=2.333…x = 2.333\ldotsx=2.333…

  1. I multiply by 10: 10x=23.333…10x = 23.333\ldots10x=23.333…
  2. I subtract: 9x=23.333…−2.333…=219x = 23.333\ldots - 2.333\ldots = 219x=23.333…−2.333…=21.
  3. I divide by 9: x=219x = \frac{21}9x=921​. I simplify by 3: x=73x = \frac 73x=37​.
  4. Check: 7 divided by 3 is 2.333…2.333\ldots2.333… ✓

(c) x=0.1212…x = 0.1212\ldotsx=0.1212… Here the period has two digits, so I multiply by 100: the point moves two places.

  1. 100x=12.1212…100x = 12.1212\ldots100x=12.1212…
  2. I subtract: 100x−x=99x=12100x - x = 99x = 12100x−x=99x=12.
  3. I divide by 99: x=1299x = \frac{12}{99}x=9912​. I simplify by 3: x=433x = \frac 4{33}x=334​.

6 · 0.9‾=10.\overline 9 = 10.9=1 with the method of exercise 5 basic

Use the same method to show that 0.999…=10.999\ldots = 10.999…=1. Then show that 5.9739‾=5.9745.973\overline 9 = 5.9745.9739=5.974.

Solution

First part. I call x=0.999…x = 0.999\ldotsx=0.999…

  1. I multiply by 10: 10x=9.999…10x = 9.999\ldots10x=9.999…
  2. I subtract: 10x−x=9.999…−0.999…=910x - x = 9.999\ldots - 0.999\ldots = 910x−x=9.999…−0.999…=9. So 9x=99x = 99x=9.
  3. I divide by 9: x=1x = 1x=1.

Second part. I split the number into two pieces: 5.9739‾=5.973+0.0009‾5.973\overline 9 = 5.973 + 0.000\overline 95.9739=5.973+0.0009.

The second piece is 0.9‾0.\overline 90.9 with the point moved three places, that is 0.9‾0.\overline 90.9 divided by 1000. Since 0.9‾=10.\overline 9 = 10.9=1, the second piece is worth 11000=0.001\frac 1{1000} = 0.00110001​=0.001.

So 5.9739‾=5.973+0.001=5.9745.973\overline 9 = 5.973 + 0.001 = 5.9745.9739=5.973+0.001=5.974.

7 · Intervals basic

(a) Write with brackets the set {x∈R∣−1<x≤3}\{x \in \R \mid -1 < x \le 3\}{x∈R∣−1<x≤3}. (b) Write with a condition the interval [0,5)[0, 5)[0,5). (c) Which interval is {x∈R∣x2<4}\{x \in \R \mid x^2 < 4\}{x∈R∣x2<4}? (d) How many elements do {0,5}\{0, 5\}{0,5} and (0,5)(0, 5)(0,5) have?

Solution

(a) (−1,3](-1, 3](−1,3]. Round on the left because −1-1−1 is excluded (<<<). Square on the right because 333 is included (≤\le≤).

(b) {x∈R∣0≤x<5}\{x \in \R \mid 0 \le x < 5\}{x∈R∣0≤x<5}. The square bracket becomes ≤\le≤, the round one becomes <<<.

(c) I look for the numbers whose square is less than 4. I try a few numbers.

  • x=1x = 1x=1: 12=11^2 = 112=1, less than 4. It works.
  • x=1.9x = 1.9x=1.9: 1.92=3.611.9^2 = 3.611.92=3.61, less than 4. It works.
  • x=2x = 2x=2: 22=42^2 = 422=4, which is not less than 4. It does not work.
  • x=−1.9x = -1.9x=−1.9: (−1.9)2=3.61(-1.9)^2 = 3.61(−1.9)2=3.61. It works: the square of a negative is positive.
  • x=−2x = -2x=−2: (−2)2=4(-2)^2 = 4(−2)2=4. It does not work.

The numbers between −2-2−2 and 222 work, without the endpoints: the interval is (−2,2)(-2, 2)(−2,2).

(d) {0,5}\{0, 5\}{0,5} has 2 elements. (0,5)(0, 5)(0,5) has infinitely many.

8 · The first terms of the sequence of eee basic

Compute as fractions a1a_1a1​, a2a_2a2​, a3a_3a3​, a4a_4a4​ of an=(1+1n)na_n = \left(1 + \frac 1n\right)^nan​=(1+n1​)n and check that they increase.

Solution

Each time I put a number in place of nnn: first I work out the brackets, then the power.

  • n=1n = 1n=1: the brackets give 1+1=21 + 1 = 21+1=2. Then 21=22^1 = 221=2. So a1=2a_1 = 2a1​=2.
  • n=2n = 2n=2: the brackets give 1+12=321 + \frac 12 = \frac 321+21​=23​. Then (32)2=94\left(\frac 32\right)^2 = \frac 94(23​)2=49​. So a2=2.25a_2 = 2.25a2​=2.25.
  • n=3n = 3n=3: the brackets give 1+13=431 + \frac 13 = \frac 431+31​=34​. Then (43)3=6427\left(\frac 43\right)^3 = \frac{64}{27}(34​)3=2764​. So a3a_3a3​ is about 2.3702.3702.370.
  • n=4n = 4n=4: the brackets give 1+14=541 + \frac 14 = \frac 541+41​=45​. Then (54)4=625256\left(\frac 54\right)^4 = \frac{625}{256}(45​)4=256625​. So a4a_4a4​ is about 2.4412.4412.441.

They increase: 2<2.25<2.370<2.4412 < 2.25 < 2.370 < 2.4412<2.25<2.370<2.441. And they stay below eee, which is about 2.7182.7182.718 (look at the graph in the section on the real numbers). Each term is a fraction, but the number they get closer and closer to is not.

9 · Field or not? intermediate

For each set, with the usual sum and product, say whether it is a field. If it is not, give one property that fails, with an example: (a) N\NN; (b) Z\ZZ; (c) the positive real numbers {x∈R∣x>0}\{x \in \R \mid x > 0\}{x∈R∣x>0}; (d) Q\QQ.

Solution

(a) N\NN: no. Rule 4 fails: the number 333 has no opposite in N\NN, because −3∉N-3 \notin \N−3∈/N.

(b) Z\ZZ: no. Rule 8 fails: the number 222 has no inverse in Z\ZZ, because 12∉Z\frac 12 \notin \Z21​∈/Z.

(c) Positive reals: no. Rule 1 fails: 000 is not positive, so the identity element of the sum is missing from the set.

(d) Q\QQ: yes. All nine rules hold. The opposite of ab\frac abba​ is −ab\frac{-a}bb−a​. If a≠0a \neq 0a=0, the inverse of ab\frac abba​ is ba\frac baab​, which is still a fraction.

10 · Calculations without a calculator intermediate

Simplify: (a) 50\sqrt{50}50​; (b) 12⋅3\sqrt{12} \cdot \sqrt 312​⋅3​; (c) 63\frac 6{\sqrt 3}3​6​; (d) (1+2)2(1 + \sqrt 2)^2(1+2​)2; (e) 12−1\frac 1{\sqrt 2 - 1}2​−11​; (f) 33\frac{\sqrt 3}333​​ and 13\frac 1{\sqrt 3}3​1​: are they equal?

Solution

(a) I look for a perfect square that divides 50: 50=25⋅250 = 25 \cdot 250=25⋅2. So 50=25⋅2=52\sqrt{50} = \sqrt{25} \cdot \sqrt 2 = 5\sqrt 250​=25​⋅2​=52​.

(b) Root times root: 12⋅3=12⋅3=36=6\sqrt{12} \cdot \sqrt 3 = \sqrt{12 \cdot 3} = \sqrt{36} = 612​⋅3​=12⋅3​=36​=6.

(c) I multiply top and bottom by 3\sqrt 33​. Top: 636\sqrt 363​. Bottom: 3⋅3=3\sqrt 3 \cdot \sqrt 3 = 33​⋅3​=3. So 633=23\frac{6\sqrt 3}3 = 2\sqrt 3363​​=23​.

(d) The square is the number times itself: (1+2)⋅(1+2)(1 + \sqrt 2) \cdot (1 + \sqrt 2)(1+2​)⋅(1+2​). I multiply each piece of the first by each piece of the second.

  • 1⋅1=11 \cdot 1 = 11⋅1=1
  • 1⋅2=21 \cdot \sqrt 2 = \sqrt 21⋅2​=2​
  • 2⋅1=2\sqrt 2 \cdot 1 = \sqrt 22​⋅1=2​
  • 2⋅2=2\sqrt 2 \cdot \sqrt 2 = 22​⋅2​=2

I add the four pieces: 1+2+2+2=3+221 + \sqrt 2 + \sqrt 2 + 2 = 3 + 2\sqrt 21+2​+2​+2=3+22​.

(e) I multiply top and bottom by 2+1\sqrt 2 + 12​+1:

12−1⋅2+12+1=2+1(2)2−12=2+12−1=2+1.\frac 1{\sqrt 2 - 1} \cdot \frac{\sqrt 2 + 1}{\sqrt 2 + 1} = \frac{\sqrt 2 + 1}{(\sqrt 2)^2 - 1^2} = \frac{\sqrt 2 + 1}{2 - 1} = \sqrt 2 + 1.2​−11​⋅2​+12​+1​=(2​)2−122​+1​=2−12​+1​=2​+1.

(f) Yes. I start from 13\frac 1{\sqrt 3}3​1​ and multiply top and bottom by 3\sqrt 33​: on top I get 3\sqrt 33​, below I get 333. So 13=33\frac 1{\sqrt 3} = \frac{\sqrt 3}33​1​=33​​. In the exam quiz the same number may appear in either form.

11 · 3\sqrt 33​ is not rational intermediate

Prove by contradiction that 3∉Q\sqrt 3 \notin \Q3​∈/Q. Hint: you need the fact "if a2a^2a2 is a multiple of 3, so is aaa". Prove this too.

Solution

The fact about multiples of 3. Dividing an integer by 3 the remainder can be 0, 1 or 2. So every integer aaa can be written in one of these three ways, where kkk is an integer: a=3ka = 3ka=3k, or a=3k+1a = 3k + 1a=3k+1, or a=3k+2a = 3k + 2a=3k+2.

I look at the square in the last two cases, those in which aaa is not a multiple of 3.

  • (3k+1)2=9k2+6k+1=3⋅(3k2+2k)+1(3k + 1)^2 = 9k^2 + 6k + 1 = 3 \cdot (3k^2 + 2k) + 1(3k+1)2=9k2+6k+1=3⋅(3k2+2k)+1. It is a multiple of 3, plus 1.
  • (3k+2)2=9k2+12k+4=3⋅(3k2+4k+1)+1(3k + 2)^2 = 9k^2 + 12k + 4 = 3 \cdot (3k^2 + 4k + 1) + 1(3k+2)2=9k2+12k+4=3⋅(3k2+4k+1)+1. This too is a multiple of 3, plus 1.

In both cases a2a^2a2 is not a multiple of 3. So, if a2a^2a2 is a multiple of 3, only the first case remains: aaa is a multiple of 3.

The proof, with the same recipe used for 2\sqrt 22​.

  1. I pretend that 3=ab\sqrt 3 = \frac ab3​=ba​, with the fraction in lowest terms.
  2. I square and get rid of the fraction: a2=3b2a^2 = 3b^2a2=3b2. So a2a^2a2 is a multiple of 3.
  3. By the fact above, aaa is a multiple of 3 too: a=3ka = 3ka=3k.
  4. I substitute: (3k)2=9k2(3k)^2 = 9k^2(3k)2=9k2, so 9k2=3b29k^2 = 3b^29k2=3b2. I divide by 3: b2=3k2b^2 = 3k^2b2=3k2.
  5. Then b2b^2b2 is a multiple of 3, and by the fact above so is bbb.
  6. aaa and bbb can both be divided by 3. But the fraction was reduced: contradiction. So 3∉Q\sqrt 3 \notin \Q3​∈/Q.

12 · Rational plus irrational intermediate

(a) Prove that if q∈Qq \in \Qq∈Q and x∉Qx \notin \Qx∈/Q, then q+x∉Qq + x \notin \Qq+x∈/Q. (b) Find two irrational numbers whose sum is rational, and two whose product is rational.

Solution

(a) In words: a fraction plus a number that is not a fraction never gives a fraction. It is proved by contradiction.

  1. I pretend that q+xq + xq+x is a fraction, and I call it rrr: q+x=rq + x = rq+x=r.
  2. I take qqq away from both sides: x=r−qx = r - qx=r−q.
  3. The difference of two fractions is a fraction. Indeed ab−cd=ad−bcbd\frac ab - \frac cd = \frac{ad - bc}{bd}ba​−dc​=bdad−bc​: top and bottom are integers.
  4. So xxx is a fraction. But we had said that xxx is not one: contradiction.

So q+xq + xq+x is not a fraction.

(b) Sum: 2+(−2)=0\sqrt 2 + (-\sqrt 2) = 02​+(−2​)=0. Product: 2⋅2=2\sqrt 2 \cdot \sqrt 2 = 22​⋅2​=2, or 2⋅8=16=4\sqrt 2 \cdot \sqrt 8 = \sqrt{16} = 42​⋅8​=16​=4.

So irrational plus irrational, and irrational times irrational, can give a rational. There is no fixed rule.

13 · 2+3\sqrt 2 + \sqrt 32​+3​ is irrational hard

(a) Prove that 6∉Q\sqrt 6 \notin \Q6​∈/Q. (b) Use it to prove that 2+3∉Q\sqrt 2 + \sqrt 3 \notin \Q2​+3​∈/Q.

Solution

(a) Same recipe.

  1. I pretend that 6=ab\sqrt 6 = \frac ab6​=ba​, a reduced fraction.
  2. I square and get rid of the fraction: a2=6b2a^2 = 6b^2a2=6b2. Since 6b2=2⋅3b26b^2 = 2 \cdot 3b^26b2=2⋅3b2, the number a2a^2a2 is even. So aaa is even: a=2ka = 2ka=2k.
  3. I substitute: 4k2=6b24k^2 = 6b^24k2=6b2. I divide by 2: 2k2=3b22k^2 = 3b^22k2=3b2.
  4. On the left there is an even number, so 3b23b^23b2 is even too. 3 is odd, and odd times odd is odd: then b2b^2b2 must be even. So bbb is even.
  5. aaa and bbb are both even, but the fraction was reduced: contradiction.

(b) By contradiction again.

  1. I pretend that 2+3\sqrt 2 + \sqrt 32​+3​ is a fraction, and I call it qqq.
  2. I square. As in exercise 10 (d), I multiply each piece by each piece:
    q2=(2)2+2⋅2⋅3+(3)2=2+26+3=5+26.q^2 = (\sqrt 2)^2 + 2 \cdot \sqrt 2 \cdot \sqrt 3 + (\sqrt 3)^2 = 2 + 2\sqrt 6 + 3 = 5 + 2\sqrt 6.q2=(2​)2+2⋅2​⋅3​+(3​)2=2+26​+3=5+26​.
  3. I isolate 6\sqrt 66​. I take away 5: q2−5=26q^2 - 5 = 2\sqrt 6q2−5=26​. I divide by 2: 6=q2−52\sqrt 6 = \frac{q^2 - 5}26​=2q2−5​.
  4. If qqq is a fraction, so is q2−52\frac{q^2 - 5}22q2−5​. So 6\sqrt 66​ would be a fraction.
  5. But by part (a) it is not: contradiction. So 2+3∉Q\sqrt 2 + \sqrt 3 \notin \Q2​+3​∈/Q.
§15

Review questions

self-check

Answer out loud or in writing, then open the answer.

What do N\NN, Z\ZZ and Q\QQ contain? Is zero in N\NN?

N\NN contains the counting numbers: 0,1,2,…0, 1, 2, \dots0,1,2,… Zero is there, in the course's convention. Z\ZZ adds the negative numbers. Q\QQ contains all the fractions ab\frac abba​ with aaa and bbb integers and bbb different from zero.

Why do we go from Q\QQ to R\RR?

Because some numbers are missing among the fractions. For example no fraction squared gives 2. And there are lists of fractions that get closer and closer to something that is not a fraction, like the list of π\piπ. The real numbers fill these "holes".

What is a Cauchy sequence, in words?

An infinite list of numbers in which, from a certain point on, the terms are as close to one another as you like. Choose a tolerance, even a tiny one: there is always a position in the list from which on any two terms are closer than that tolerance.

How are the real numbers defined with Cauchy sequences?

A real number is a list of fractions that tightens (a Cauchy sequence). Two lists that get closer and closer to the same thing count as the same number. If the list gets closer and closer to a fraction, it represents that fraction. Otherwise it defines a new number, an irrational one.

What does it mean that R\RR is complete?

That it has no holes. Every list of real numbers that tightens gets closer and closer to a real number. Redoing the construction starting from R\RR you find no new number.

Repeat the proof that 2\sqrt 22​ is not rational.

By contradiction 2=ab\sqrt 2 = \frac ab2​=ba​, a reduced fraction. Squaring: a2=2b2a^2 = 2b^2a2=2b2. So a2a^2a2 is even and aaa is even too: a=2ka = 2ka=2k. Substituting, 4k2=2b24k^2 = 2b^24k2=2b2, that is b2=2k2b^2 = 2k^2b2=2k2. So bbb is even too. Then aaa and bbb can both be divided by 2, but the fraction was reduced: contradiction.

What is a field? Give an example and a counterexample.

A set with a sum and a product that obey the nine rules: the identity elements 0 and 1, the opposites, the inverses of the numbers different from zero, the commutative, associative and distributive properties. Examples: Q\QQ, R\RR, C\CC. Counterexample: Z\ZZ, because 2 has no inverse among the integers.

Why does zero have no inverse?

The inverse of 0 should be a number that, multiplied by 0, gives 1. But every number multiplied by 0 gives 0. That is why rule 8 asks for the inverse only for the numbers different from zero.

How is a>ba > ba>b defined?

a>ba > ba>b when a−ba - ba−b is positive. So it is enough to know which numbers are positive. In Z\ZZ they are 1,2,3,…1, 2, 3, \dots1,2,3,… In Q\QQ they are the fractions in which top and bottom have the same sign.

What is the difference between {1,2}\{1, 2\}{1,2}, (1,2)(1, 2)(1,2) and [1,2][1, 2][1,2]?

{1,2}\{1, 2\}{1,2} is the set with the two elements 1 and 2. (1,2)(1, 2)(1,2) is the open interval: all the real numbers between 1 and 2, endpoints excluded. It can also be a point or a vector, depending on the context. [1,2][1, 2][1,2] is the closed interval: endpoints included.

Which are the nine Greek letters to know?

α\alphaα (alpha), ε\varepsilonε (epsilon), σ\sigmaσ (sigma), ϑ\varthetaϑ (theta), ϕ\phiϕ (phi), π\piπ (pi), λ\lambdaλ (lambda), μ\muμ (mu), ϱ\varrhoϱ (rho).

How do you remove a root from the number below in a fraction?

Multiply top and bottom by the same root: 63=633=23\frac 6{\sqrt 3} = \frac{6\sqrt 3}3 = 2\sqrt 33​6​=363​​=23​. If there is a difference such as 2−1\sqrt 2 - 12​−1 below, multiply top and bottom by 2+1\sqrt 2 + 12​+1: below you get (2)2−12=1(\sqrt 2)^2 - 1^2 = 1(2​)2−12=1.

§16

Glossary

terms
Set
A bag of objects, which are called elements. It is written with curly brackets: {1,3,5}\{1, 3, 5\}{1,3,5}. Order and repetitions do not matter.
Membership (∈\in∈)
3∈A3 \in A3∈A means that 3 is an element of AAA. The opposite is written ∉\notin∈/.
Subset (⊂\subset⊂)
B⊂AB \subset AB⊂A means that every element of BBB is also in AAA. With ⊊\subsetneq⊊ we add that AAA has something more.
Natural numbers N\NN
The counting numbers: 0,1,2,3,…0, 1, 2, 3, \dots0,1,2,3,… Zero is included.
Integers Z\ZZ
The naturals plus the negative numbers: …,−2,−1,0,1,2,…\dots, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, \dots…,−2,−1,0,1,2,…
Rational numbers Q\QQ
The numbers that can be written as a fraction of two integers, with the number below different from zero. As decimals they end or repeat.
Real numbers R\RR
The numbers that may have infinitely many digits after the point. Precisely: lists of fractions that get closer and closer to one another.
Irrational number
A real number that is not a fraction, such as 2\sqrt 22​, π\piπ, eee.
Sequence
An infinite list of numbers, one after the other: a1,a2,a3,…a_1, a_2, a_3, \dotsa1​,a2​,a3​,…
Cauchy sequence
A sequence in which, from a certain position on, the terms are closer to one another than any chosen tolerance.
Completeness
The property of R\RR of having no holes: every Cauchy sequence gets closer and closer to a real number. Q\QQ is not complete.
Proof by contradiction
You pretend that the opposite of what you want to prove is true and you reach something impossible.
Binary operation
A rule that takes two numbers and gives back one, like the sum and the product.
Identity element
The number that changes nothing: 0 for the sum, 1 for the product.
Opposite
The opposite of aaa is −a-a−a: added together they give 0. For example the opposite of 7 is −7-7−7.
Inverse
The inverse of aaa is a−1a^{-1}a−1, that is 1a\frac 1aa1​: multiplied together they give 1. Zero has no inverse.
Field
A set with a sum and a product that obey the nine rules of Proposition 1.5. Q\QQ, R\RR and C\CC are; N\NN and Z\ZZ are not.
Order
a>ba > ba>b when a−ba - ba−b is positive. R\RR is ordered, C\CC is not.
Interval
A piece of the number line. (a,b)(a, b)(a,b) excludes the endpoints, [a,b][a, b][a,b] includes them.
Quantifiers
The symbols ∀\forall∀ and ∃\exists∃: they read "for every" and "there exists".

  • The explanations in words, the examples with numbers, the "Refresher" and "Your turn" boxes and the exercises belong to these notes. The "Beyond the handouts" parts (repeating decimals, reading the symbols, calculating with roots) connect the lesson to the rest of the course and to the exam.
